facts.text: L. L. Zamenhof grew up in Bialystok, then part of the Russian Empire and now in Poland.
In Zamenhof's youth, Bialystok was home to Poles, Germans, Russians and Yiddish-speaking Jews; each group spoke its own language and regarded the others with suspicion.
Zamenhof himself spoke Yiddish, Russian, German, French, Hebrew, Latin and English.
Zamenhof trained as a doctor at medical school in Moscow, where he studied in his twenties.
Zamenhof hoped that a shared neutral language would help people of different religions and ethnic groups understand one another and support world peace.
On July 26, 1887, Zamenhof published the first Esperanto textbook, Unua Libro (First Book).
He published the book under a pen name, Doktoro Esperanto, meaning one who hopes; the language later took its name from this pen name.
The first book set out 16 basic grammar rules and included a dictionary; it was soon translated into more than a dozen languages.
Esperanto's word roots came from European languages such as English, French, German, Greek, Italian, Latin, Polish, Russian and Yiddish.
Zamenhof meant the language to be learnable in about three weeks by people with many different mother tongues.

Seven years before Esperanto, a German Catholic priest had tried to spread an invented language called Volapuk; it died out, partly because its creator wanted to keep control of every decision about it.
Zamenhof, by contrast, released the language and did not interfere with how its speakers went on to use and develop it.
The first international Esperanto congress was held in August 1905 at Boulogne-sur-Mer, France, and speakers have met at world congresses every year since then.
When the sixth international congress opened in Washington, D.C., in August 1910, there were an estimated 2.5 million Esperanto speakers worldwide.

After World War I an Iranian delegate proposed Esperanto as a language of international relations at the League of Nations, but the French delegate blocked it, fearing French would lose its standing in diplomacy.
In 1922 the French government banned the teaching of Esperanto at French universities.
In the 1930s, under Hitler and Stalin, Esperanto speakers were treated as suspects and many were persecuted.
Scholar Humphrey Tonkin links Esperanto to an early wave of globalism that was destroyed by the rise of nationalism in the early 20th century.
Zamenhof was nominated 14 times for the Nobel Peace Prize between 1907 and his death in 1917, but never won.
UNESCO recognized the Universal Esperanto Association in a 1954 resolution and in 1985 encouraged countries to add Esperanto to school courses.
Today perhaps as many as two million people around the world speak Esperanto.
By 2016 Esperanto was spoken in over 120 countries and its Wikipedia had over 230,000 articles.
Esperanto never became a widely spoken everyday language, though its ideals have kept a community of speakers going.
